name: Ascorbyl tetraisopalmitate

card.summary: Ascorbyl tetraisopalmitate is an oil-soluble, stable form of vitamin C used in serums and sunscreens to brighten skin, even tone and support a smoother, younger-looking complexion.
card.note: Studies of it are mainly in combination formulas, often by the formulators.

quick.overview:
Ascorbyl tetraisopalmitate (ATIP) is a vitamin C derivative that dissolves in oil, which makes it more stable than plain ascorbic acid and easier to blend into creams and serums. People use it for brighter, more even skin tone, less visible pigmentation and a smoother look.

In published trials it appears inside multi-ingredient formulas: a 24-person study of a night serum with melatonin and bakuchiol reported improvements in texture, pigmentation and wrinkles, and a 60-person randomized trial of sunscreens with ATIP and rice peptides reported better hydration and less hyperpigmentation.
quick.how: It is applied topically as part of leave-on serums, moisturizers or sunscreens, usually daily. Formulas often pair it with other antioxidants, retinoid-like actives or sunscreen filters. Skin changes in the trials appeared over 12 weeks or more.
quick.risks: Topical vitamin C derivatives are generally regarded as well tolerated. Studies report improvements without major safety signals, but they are small and mostly of combination products, so effects of ATIP alone are less clear.

lead: Ascorbyl tetraisopalmitate (ATIP) is an oil-soluble ester of vitamin C used in skincare. A 2025 laboratory paper describes it as having better stability and transdermal absorption than plain vitamin C, with potential for skin whitening and wound healing.[1]

In looksmaxxing and skincare, it is used to brighten skin, reduce hyperpigmentation and support collagen-related antioxidant protection against sun damage. Because it dissolves in oil rather than water, it can be formulated into creams and sunscreens without the quick oxidation that affects ascorbic acid solutions.[1]
Human studies have mostly tested formulas that contain it alongside other ingredients, such as melatonin and bakuchiol in a night serum, or rice peptides in sunscreens.[2][3]

chain: Oil-soluble vitamin C applied to skin
Antioxidant action and support for collagen pathways
Brighter, more even and smoother skin
angle.text: ATIP is used in leave-on products to even out pigmentation and improve texture. Trials of formulas containing it report better skin quality scores, hydration and less hyperpigmentation.

paras: Cosmetic uses center on skin brightening, pigmentation, and signs of photoaging. A 2026 systematic review in the Journal of Clinical and Aesthetic Dermatology covers clinical applications of vitamin C in dermatology broadly.[4]

Ascorbic acid increases collagen gene expression and collagen I levels in cultured dermal fibroblasts.[5] Compared with the parent molecule, ATIP is described as more stable and better absorbed through skin, though low water solubility and storage needs limit some uses, which research groups are addressing with nanocarriers.[1][6][7]

A molecular dynamics simulation modeled ATIP moving through the hair follicle infundibulum and the stratum corneum.[8] A gene-expression study of a melatonin, bakuchiol and ATIP serum reported it modulates UV-related signaling in skin.[9]

In a multicenter study, 24 subjects applied a night serum containing melatonin, bakuchiol and ATIP nightly for 12 weeks, with 12 continuing to 24 weeks. Dermatologists rated global aesthetic improvement of +1.21 points at 12 weeks and +1.25 at 24 weeks, with significant improvement in texture, pigmentation, erythema, tone, lines and wrinkles.[2] Dermal and epidermal thickness rose without reaching statistical significance.[2]

A double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial in 60 women aged 20-30 with early photoaging found that daily sunscreens and cosmetics containing ATIP and rice peptides increased skin hydration and dermis echogenicity, reduced hyperpigmentation and increased epidermal cell renewal.[3]
Animal and laboratory work has examined ATIP-loaded nanoparticles and fibers for wound healing, including a mouse model of wound closure.[1][6]
